title: Notes: what an item is, why it costs what it does and what to check; where to spend, where to save
status: Each note's sources were read on their pages on 04-10-2026 (E2) and the note cut to what they say: checked marks a note whose every fact is on its sources' pages, with any reasoning of our own cited as own; own marks a note that is our own rule, its reason given in it (T1, D-UX-34).

what.text: The finish on the floor, with its skirting: vitrified tiles or large slabs fixed on adhesive, or natural stone such as marble, laid in mortar and polished on site.

cost.text: Tiles cost more as they grow larger, and large slabs need adhesive on a flat base. Marble is polished after laying, and again every five to ten years in a home.

check.text: Vitrified tiles: IS 15622, water absorption 0.5% or less. Marble: look at the back of each slab and for resin-filled lines, and tap it: a dull or hollow sound means gaps or cracks.

what.text: The finish on inside walls and ceilings: wall putty to smooth the plaster, a primer, and two coats of emulsion paint.

cost.text: On an economy emulsion the labour costs about as much as the paint; on a luxury one the paint costs most. Dearer emulsions stand more scrubbing and are reported to last longer between repaints.

check.text: Ask for the whole system on the quote: putty, a primer, and two coats of the named emulsion.

what.text: The outside walls of a house: cracks and gaps filled, an exterior primer that resists the alkali in plaster, then a weatherproof emulsion or a texture finish.

cost.text: A texture finish costs more than an emulsion and is reported to last longer: 8 to 15 years, against 5 to 8.

check.text: Ask for the paint's name and the number of coats on the quote, and ask the engineer to look at any wide or growing crack before it is filled.

what.text: The bathroom's taps and mixers, the shower and the health faucet, with the angle valves that feed them. A concealed diverter or thermostatic valve sits inside the wall; only its plate shows.

cost.text: Solid brass fittings cost more than stainless steel or ABS plastic ones, and the finish (chrome, matte black, gold or brushed) changes the price.

check.text: Before a concealed valve or pipe is tiled over, ask for a pressure test held for 30 minutes with no leak and no drop in pressure.

what.text: The kitchen's base and wall units: boxes (carcasses) with shutters and hardware, priced by the running foot of base and wall units together.

cost.text: The shutters' finish leads: laminate costs least, then high-gloss acrylic, then PU lacquer and lacquered glass. Membrane (PVC foil) is a budget finish on MDF in one guide and priced with the dearest in another. Then the fittings: soft-close hinges, tandem drawers, pull-outs and corner units.

check.text: BWP plywood (IS 710 on its edge) under the sink, and the edges sealed with banding. Membrane (PVC foil) can peel at the edges in heat and humidity, so keep it away from the hob.

what.text: A built-in wardrobe: a box (the carcass) with hinged or sliding shutters, and the hardware that moves them: hinges, channels, sliding tracks, handles and soft-close dampers.

cost.text: The shutters' finish sets most of the price: laminate costs least, then membrane, acrylic and PU, and veneer or lacquered glass most. Then the board and the hardware.

check.text: Read the standard printed on the board's edge: IS 303 for MR or BWR plywood, IS 710 for BWP, so 'BWR 710' mixes the two and is a warning sign. At a cut edge the layers should be tightly packed, without gaps, and the edges sealed with banding.

what.text: Storage built in for good, such as a TV unit, a crockery unit or a shoe rack, made as a wardrobe is: a box with shutters and hardware.

cost.text: As with a wardrobe, the shutters' finish sets most of the price: laminate costs least, then membrane, acrylic and PU, and veneer or lacquered glass most; then the board and the hardware.

check.text: Read the standard on the board's edge (IS 303 for MR or BWR, IS 710 for BWP) and ask for BWP by the sink. Seal every cut edge with banding; the layers at an edge should be tightly packed, without gaps.

what.text: A three-seater sofa, built in four layers: a frame, a suspension, foam cushions, and a cover of fabric or leather.

cost.text: The frame, the foam and the cover set the price. A frame of seasoned (kiln-dried) hardwood such as sheesham, sal or teak lasts; avoid one of thin particle board or MDF. Denser foam costs more to make but lasts three to four times longer.

check.text: Ask what the frame is made of and whether the wood is kiln-dried. Seat foam: 32 kg a cubic metre or denser. Fabric for daily use: rated for tens of thousands of rubs (Martindale).

what.text: The bars inside the concrete of the columns, beams and slabs. TMT means thermo-mechanically treated; Fe 500D, a yield strength of at least 500 MPa, the D marking bars that stretch further before they break (16% or more, against 12% for Fe 500).

cost.text: Steel's price moves often. How much a house takes follows its structural design: spans, foundation, soil and seismic zone. A rule of thumb is only a first estimate until the engineer's design.

check.text: The licence number (CM/L) on the bundle's tag, the grade on the bar, and a mill test certificate for each load. A 12 mm bar weighs about 0.89 kg a metre; one well short is thinner than its size. Have the structural engineer check the bars before each pour.

spendSave.text: The foundation, the frame and the slabs cannot be redone once the house stands. The steel in them should follow the structural engineer's drawings; a rule of thumb is only a first estimate.
A leak under finished tiles means breaking the tiles and plaster and redoing the floor. Ask for a flood test of 24 to 48 hours on each bathroom floor before the tiles go down.
Paint is the easiest finish to change: walls are repainted every few years anyway, so a premium emulsion now can become a luxury one at the next repaint.
A concealed diverter or thermostatic valve sits behind the tiles, so changing it later means breaking them. Taps, showers and basins on the surface can be upgraded later.
Replacing a window frame later means making good the wall, plaster and finishes round it.

It runs in pipes under the plaster, and adding a circuit to a plastered house later is costly and messy. Mark where the furniture goes before the walls are cut, and ask for ISI-marked FRLS copper wire (IS 694).
They fit on points already wired, so they can be changed or upgraded later without touching the walls.

The pipes run inside the walls and under the floors, so a leak found later means breaking tiles. Ask for a pressure test of every line, held 30 minutes without a leak or a drop, before the walls are closed and tiled.
Furniture moves in and out without work on the house, so it can be bought in stages or upgraded later as money allows.
Curtains and other soft furnishings can be changed at any time without work on the house.
